Q104173683.summary: This long marble lid is divided into a row of panels with pairs of figures in low relief. According to the museum, Christ appears in several of them: at the far left changing water into wine at Cana, at the centre raising the dead (Lazarus or the widow's son of Nain) between drawn-back curtains, and at the right multiplying the loaves. Together the miracles of wine and bread evoked the Eucharist and the hope of resurrection.
facts: In the 18th century the curtains were mistaken for goose feet and the scene for a palace murder, so the lid was linked to the legendary 'Queen Pédauque' (the goose-footed queen).
It was reused for centuries as a door lintel at the church of La Daurade in Toulouse, leading to the cemetery of the Counts of Toulouse, before entering the museum's collections by 1805.
The lid is about 2.15 m long.
Q104173683.notes: The thumbnail is small; scene identifications follow the museum's description. The worklist tag 'Wedding at Cana' is correct for one panel only.
Q104173683.original_title: Couvercle du sarcophage dit de la Reine Pédauque

Q116409987.summary: Though heavily damaged, this limestone frieze still shows Christ enthroned under an arch at the centre, stretching out his right hand over a heap of baskets. Angels stand at his left and right, and beyond them apostles or saints hold books and raise their hands as if preaching. The baskets recall the twelve that were left over when Christ fed the five thousand.
facts: It is said to come from Bawit in Middle Egypt, site of a major early monastery.
The fragment is about a metre long and weighs some 51 kg.
It came to the Met in 1910 (Rogers Fund).
